title: Lesson 26: Enterprise REST API Design: Versioning, Pagination, Bulk, and Best Practices
description: The design layer under every REST integration: how Salesforce versions its API, how to page through large result sets without breaking, when bulk writes beat synchronous calls, and the habits that keep an integration alive for years.

questions.question: Why is walking a large result set with the server's next-page pointer safer than requesting a numbered range of rows?
options: The pointer returns the entire result set in one response, so no loop is required.
The pointer lets a client page through results without ever checking whether more rows remain.
The pointer stays stable when rows are added or removed mid-walk, unlike a numbered range.
The pointer always needs fewer API calls than requesting a numbered range.
questions.explanation: A cursor tracks a fixed position on the server, so inserts or deletes behind the scenes do not shift the set out from under the client the way a numbered offset does.

questions.question: A nightly job must sync tens of thousands of records, while an on-screen action creates one record and needs its ID back at once. Which approach fits each?
options: A bulk ingest job for the nightly sync and a single synchronous call for the on-screen create.
A single synchronous call for both, looped over every record for the nightly sync.
A bulk ingest job for both, since asynchronous always beats synchronous.
A batched synchronous call for the nightly sync and a bulk job for the single on-screen create.
questions.explanation: Match the tool to the latency the work actually needs: high-volume scheduled writes go async in bulk, while an interactive action that needs an immediate answer stays on a single synchronous call.

questions.question: Why does pinning an API version in the request path not remove the need for maintenance?
options: Because the version in the path is ignored once a newer release ships.
Because each pinned version supports only one consumer at a time.
Because pinned versions are retired on a schedule, so pinning schedules the upgrade.
Because pinning forces every consumer of the org onto the newest version the moment it releases.
questions.explanation: A pinned version holds its behavior steady, but the platform retires old versions on a schedule, so pinning schedules the upgrade instead of eliminating it.
